recall.question: How do U07 concepts map to sessions?

keyTerms.definition: A line between what the agent may touch and what it may not.
System outranks developer, developer outranks user, user outranks tool outputs.
Tool output is data, never instructions.

recall.answer: The trust boundary separates what the agent may touch from what it may not. The instruction hierarchy ranks system > developer > user > tool outputs. Tool output is data, never instructions.
recall.question: What are the trust rules?

sections.title: Local remediation: trust, instructions, capabilities, consent

keyTerms.definition: Stop a tool output from hijacking the agent; the major mechanism of U07.
100 tool outputs, 5 poisoned; naive obeys 4, defended obeys 0.
Any text from tools, files, or web pages.

recall.answer: Shell 0 asks how to stop tool outputs from hijacking the agent. Shell 1 builds the 100-output toy: naive obeys 4 of 5 poisoned, defended marks all as data and obeys 0. Shell 2 defines the untrusted span.
recall.question: What does the injection-defense ladder build?

sections.title: Russian-doll ladder for the major mechanism (injection defense)

keyTerms.definition: Answered in C01.
Answered in C02.
Answered in C05.

recall.answer: What the agent may read (C01), how attacks arrive (C02), how to test defenses (C03), where the boundary sits (C04), when a human decides (C05), how coding agents are judged (C06, C07), crash survival (C08), and user models (C09).
recall.question: What does the dependency list resolve?

keyTerms.definition: Rules for what the agent may read, keep, and share.
Touch only what the task needs.
Log every data touch with its class and need; flag touches without need.

recall.answer: 20 tasks, data classes public/internal/secret. The agent touches secret data it does not need. The audit flags the violation. Without labeling, the audit reports 0 violations and misses everything.
recall.question: How do privacy norms work?

keyTerms.definition: The user says ignore your instructions.
A tool output, file, or web page carries the instruction.
Every span carries its source; the planner refuses tool/web instructions.

recall.answer: 100 tool outputs, 5 poisoned. Naive agent obeys 4 of 5. Tagging agent marks all 100 as data and obeys 0, with 0 clean tasks broken.
recall.question: How does tagging defeat injection?

keyTerms.definition: Adversarial testing; attackers think in exceptions.
Fraction of attacks achieving the attacker's goal; 0.24 then 0.06 in the toy.
Generate attacks, count successes, fix the top failure, repeat.

recall.answer: 50 crafted attacks, 12 succeed: ASR 0.24. After the tagging fix: 3 succeed: ASR 0.06. The loop found the gap and measured the fix.
recall.question: What does the red-team loop measure?

keyTerms.definition: The check: intercept every tool call, test membership in K.
Capability set K; allowed iff a in K.
Works even when the model is confused, injected, or malicious.

recall.answer: Capabilities {read}. 20 tasks: 14 need read only, 6 need send. The 6 are denied at the boundary. Enforcement at the action layer works even when the model is confused.
recall.question: How does the boundary enforce?

keyTerms.definition: Sort actions by reversibility and blast radius.
The agent proposes, the human disposes.
auto, approve, block; assumes the human reviews carefully.

recall.answer: Auto (read-only), approve (writes under $100), block (deletes, sends). 100 actions: 60 auto, 30 approve, 10 block. Click-through approvers make the tier theater.
recall.question: What are the approval tiers?

keyTerms.definition: Read the issue, write code, run tests, read failures, fix, repeat.
The repo, the test command, and the sandbox.
Tests are the only scalable judge of code.

recall.answer: 20 tasks, one patch each. The test rig runs the suite: 14 pass (0.70). The test rig is the judge, not the agent's self-assessment. Weak tests certify broken code.
recall.question: Who judges the coding agent?

keyTerms.definition: Real issues from real repos with real test suites.
Tests that fail before and pass after the fix.
Tests that must keep passing.

recall.answer: 20 real GitHub issues. The agent fixes 8: 0.40. It proves the agent can fix real bugs with tests; it does not prove design judgment. The fix must flip FAIL_TO_PASS without breaking PASS_TO_PASS.
recall.question: What does SWE-bench prove?

keyTerms.definition: A saved state the run can resume from.
Serialize the state; on crash reload the latest.
n steps; max loss n steps, average n/2.

recall.answer: The agent crashes at step 47 of 100. Without checkpoints, 47 steps are lost. With interval 10, at most 10 steps are lost (5 on average). The tradeoff: frequent checkpoints cost time and storage.
recall.question: What do checkpoints save?

keyTerms.definition: The agent's picture of the user: goals, preferences, constraints, context.
(attribute, value, confidence, source).
Each observation updates confidence; corrections override.

recall.answer: 5 preferences: concise answers, Python, no emails after 5pm, plots over tables, and one more. Built from statements, behavior, and corrections. Always uncertain; confidence tells the agent when to ask.
recall.question: What is in the toy user model?

keyTerms.definition: From reactive to proactive: predict what the user will do and prepare.
Fraction of top predictions correct; 62/100 in the toy.
A wrong proactive action costs more than no action.

recall.answer: 100 mornings, predicts run tests each time, correct 62 times: precision 0.62. The most common next action in this context wins. A correct but unwanted prediction (tests on a broken build) still fails.
recall.question: How is next-action scored?

keyTerms.definition: Control passes back and forth between agent and user.
Propose, decide, act, with interruption rights.
Agent or user per step; either side may pause.

recall.answer: The agent proposes 3 flight options (agent initiative), the user picks one (user initiative), the agent books it. The agent takes initiative when confident and stakes are low; the user when choice needs taste.
recall.question: How does the flight toy split initiative?

keyTerms.definition: The user's permission, scaled to the stakes.
Built by staying in bounds and stating uncertainty.
None, implicit, explicit-once, explicit-each-time.

recall.answer: Read: implicit ok. Write draft: implicit ok. Send to colleague: explicit once. Send to boss: explicit each time. One rule for all actions either paralyzes or endangers.
recall.question: What is the consent gradient?

keyTerms.definition: Privacy norms, permission boundary, approval tiers bound the action space.
Injection defense and red-teaming test the walls.
User models, next-action, mixed initiative, consent.

recall.answer: Privacy norms, permission boundaries, and approval tiers bound the action space. Injection defense and red-teaming test the walls. Coding agents get a test rig and provenance-aware scores, long runs get checkpoints, and proactive agents model the user with consent.
recall.question: What is the arc of U07?
